syllabus.clause: searching a monotone predicate over the answer space (capacity, rate, threshold)

at.step: The candidate space is now capacities, not array indices; the predicate is "is this capacity enough," checked by a greedy packing pass instead of a comparison. The half-open range, the loop invariant and the overflow-safe midpoint all carry over from the previous topic unchanged — only what counts as the predicate is different.

A packing feasibility check — does this capacity need at most this many trips — is monotone in capacity, so binary search on it is safe. What happens if a caller hands binary search a predicate that isn't actually monotone?

A genuinely non-monotone predicate — true, false, true, true, false — handed to the identical loop: the loop still terminates and returns index two, confidently. But the array's first true position is index zero, which the search never even examines, because the loop's own correctness proof assumes a single boundary that this predicate doesn't have.

syllabus.clause: real-valued bisection and its iteration count

at.step: The same idea over a continuous range instead of integers: there is no "next" real number to converge to exactly, so the loop stops at a precision bound instead of an empty range. Bisecting for the square root of two, narrowing from one and two toward one point four one four two.
Halve the required precision — does the number of iterations double, stay the same, or something else entirely?

The iteration count to reach a given precision on a real-valued range is the ceiling of log base two of the span divided by epsilon — the identical halving argument from the previous topic, now over a continuous range, and completely indifferent to how expensive the predicate itself is to evaluate.

Megiddo's own framing, from 1983: a decision procedure — does a value at least this good exist — composed with an outer binary search over candidate values gives an optimisation procedure that finds the best one. Every worked example in this topic has been an instance of exactly this pattern, which Megiddo himself notes is not always the fastest route to a given answer, only often the best known one for harder problems.
